blocks.prompt: 11 (a) A rock is dropped from a cliff. One second later, another rock is dropped from the same height. What is the distance between the two rocks 2 seconds after the first rock is dropped?
blocks.explanation:
Two free falls from rest, the second starting 1 s later.
Given: \(u = 0\) for both, \(a = g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2\) downward. Find: the gap when the first rock has fallen for 2 s.
Plan: the first rock has fallen for 2 s, the second for only 1 s; find each fall with \(x = \frac{1}{2}gt^2\) and subtract.
steps:
Given: both rocks start from rest (\(u = 0\)) at the same point; \(a = g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2\) (downward positive); the second rock is dropped 1 s after the first.
To find: the distance between the rocks at \(t = 2\) s after the first rock is dropped.
Method: Measure \(t\) from the first drop. Use \(x = ut + \frac{1}{2}gt^2\) for each rock with its own falling time. Both fall along the same vertical line, so the distance between them is the difference of the distances fallen. We assume the cliff is high enough that neither rock has landed.

Distance fallen by each rock
\[x_1 = \dfrac{1}{2}(9.8)t^2 = 4.9t^2\]
\[x_2 = 4.9(t - 1)^2,\quad t \ge 1\]
Why: The second rock has been falling for only \(t - 1\) seconds.

Put t = 2
\[x_1 = 4.9(2)^2 = 19.6\ \text{m}\]
\[x_2 = 4.9(1)^2 = 4.9\ \text{m}\]
Why: At \(t = 2\) the first rock has fallen for 2 s and the second for 1 s.

Distance between the rocks
\[x_1 - x_2 = 19.6 - 4.9\]
\[= 14.7\ \text{m}\]
Why: Both are below the same point on one vertical line, so the gap is the difference of their falls.

Check
\[t = 1:\ \text{gap} = 4.9\ \text{m}\]
\[\text{gap} = 4.9 + 9.8(1) = 14.7\ \text{m}\ \checkmark\]
Why: At \(t = 1\) the first rock has fallen 4.9 m and moves at \(9.8\) m/s. After that both have the same acceleration, so the first rock stays exactly 9.8 m/s faster and the gap grows by 9.8 m in the next second.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The book prints no answer for Exercise 7.1, so this answer is ours. It was checked independently with a computer algebra system and against an independent worked solution.

blocks.prompt: 11 (b) A rock is dropped from a cliff. One second later, another rock is dropped from the same height. At what time will the distance between them be 14.7 m?
blocks.explanation:
Same set-up as part (a), but now the gap is given and the time is unknown.
Given: gap \(= 14.7\) m. Find: the time \(t\) after the first rock is dropped.
Plan: write the gap as a formula in \(t\), simplify, set it equal to 14.7 and solve.
steps:
Given: \(x_1 = 4.9t^2\) and \(x_2 = 4.9(t - 1)^2\) from part (a) (\(t\) measured from the first drop); gap \(d = 14.7\) m.
To find: the time \(t\).
Method: Form \(d = x_1 - x_2\), simplify it, and solve \(d = 14.7\).

Gap as a function of t
\[d = 4.9t^2 - 4.9(t - 1)^2\]
\[= 4.9[t^2 - (t^2 - 2t + 1)]\]
\[= 4.9(2t - 1)\]
Why: \((t - 1)^2 = t^2 - 2t + 1\); the \(t^2\) terms cancel, so the gap grows steadily with time.

The answer must have t at least 1
\[0 \le t < 1:\ d = 4.9t^2 < 4.9\]
Why: Before \(t = 1\) the second rock is still at the top, so the gap is less than 4.9 m and cannot be 14.7 m. So the formula of the last step applies.

Solve
\[4.9(2t - 1) = 14.7\]
\[2t - 1 = 3\]
\[t = 2\ \text{s}\]
Why: Divide both sides by 4.9 (\(14.7 = 3 \times 4.9\)).

Check
\[x_1 - x_2 = 19.6 - 4.9 = 14.7\ \text{m}\ \checkmark\]
Why: This is exactly part (a): at \(t = 2\) s the gap is 14.7 m.
blocks.final_answer: \(t = 2\) s after the first rock is dropped (that is, 1 s after the second rock is dropped).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The book prints no answer for Exercise 7.1, so this answer is ours. It was checked independently with a computer algebra system and against an independent worked solution. Part (b) is part (a) read backwards, so getting \(t = 2\) s again is a good sign.
